newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai banks face slowing growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Thai banks face slowing growth in 1997.

text.p: Thai banks will face a slowdown in earnings growth during the first half of 1997 as profits are hit by provisioning requirements to cover declining loan portfolio quality, analysts said on Wednesday.
With the Thai economy set to grow at its lowest level in a decade and a bursting property bubble, banks would face increasing loan defaults, analysts said.

"The question is whether they will boost provisioning or write them off and take a hit. My fear is that they will hang on hoping the government comes in with some scheme and drag it out for years," said Scott Christiansen, bank analyst at Jardine Fleming Thanakom Securities.
Christiansen said serious attempts to address loan problems could see banks' profit growth as low as 2.0 percent in 1997.
A recent Solomon Brothers report suggested that 25 percent of loans to the property sector would become non-performing.
Estimates of property exposure in the Thai banking sector ranged between six and 20 percent of total loan portfolios.
Bangkok Bank, Krung Thai Bank, Thai Farmers Bank and Siam Commercial Bank, the four largest banks, are said to have exposures below an industry average of 10 percent, however.
A sharply decelerating Thai economy, which private economists say will grow by less than seven percent this year -- its lowest level in a decade -- has increased worries about bank profitability.
"There are some genuine concerns at the speed at which the economy has slowed down. I think it has taken some by surprise," said James Marshall, head of research at Capital Nomura Securities.
"But I think the situation is manageable, it's what you would expect," he said, adding that Nomura sees bank profit growth in 1997 at under 10 percent.
Export growth running at 2.4 percent in the first eight months of 1996 compared with 24 percent in 1995 also has nerves on edge.
"There are problems with some loans in the manufacturing sector where banks have 25-35 percent of their loans," said a senior bank analyst at a Thai broker.
"A lot of firms are suffering at the moment given the export slowdown, and I don't see it getting better quickly," he said.
On top of this is a liquidity crunch caused by some of the highest interest rates in Asia. This is good for bank margins, analysts say, but it heightens the risks of loan defaults.

"All the signs point to liquidity staying tight. I see a maximum 100 basis points off interest rates by mid-1997, but I think margin spreads will widen," said Tanawat Patchimkul, banking analyst at Seamico Securities.
"I don't think it will get much worse, but the economy could go one of two ways," he said.
That final possibility has some local brokers reviewing overweight recommendations on local bank stocks.
